purpose: Primary-source collection for possible gap coverage. This is not a campaign selection or architectural recommendation.
method: Read the cited primary-source passages in online translations/transcriptions; distinguish source assertions from later calendrical conversion and editorial framing. URLs below are candidates actually consulted, except where marked otherwise. No map or terrain claim was checked.

candidates.event: Valentinian and Valens' order affecting Alexandrian bishops, Athanasius' concealed departure, and imperial recall/return

primarySource.title: Historia Acephala (anonymous Alexandrian chronicle)
primarySource.coverageActuallyRead: Read page lines/paragraphs X.15 through XI.16, including decree dated Pachon 10, Coss. Valentinian and Valens; Athanasius' Paophi 8 flight to a villa near the New River; imperial recall and entry into the Dionysius church on Mechir 7. Also checked XII.17 for a separate death date, not used as the principal locator here.
primarySource.sourceDateAsStated: The order was delivered in Alexandria on Pachon 10 in the consulate of Valentinian and Valens; the edition renders May 5, 365. The annal says return occurred on Mechir 7 in the consulate of Gratian and Dagalaifus (366). It says four months and twenty-four days after the account's prior events for the secret departure, with Egyptian month dates.
primarySource.editorialDateOrConversion: 365 and 366 are consular-year conversions supplied in the translation/editorial presentation; do not call parenthetical dates proleptic Gregorian. Month/day conversions follow the edition, and Egyptian civil-calendar alignment needs separate calendrical checking.
primarySource.narratorDateAndAge: Anonymous compiler; age unknown. The annalistic and administrative detail may preserve near-contemporary Alexandrian records, but this passage does not identify an eyewitness author or establish that the compiler witnessed the events.

localGeography: villa near the New River (local hydronym rendered by the translation)
whatItCanSupport: The chronicle reports an imperial order to eject bishops restored under Julian, coupled with a fine on officials.
It reports Athanasius secretly leaving and later being recalled by an imperial letter and escorted back to a named church.
The source supplies Egyptian month/day and consular dating useful for a dated event candidate.
whatItDoesNotProve: That every detail is independently corroborated or eyewitness testimony.
A single, universally accepted modern-calendar date without calendar-conversion analysis.
The exact archaeological identification or location of the ‘New River’ villa or the Dionysius church.
A simple uninterrupted narrative of policy: this source reports local orders and administrative actions, not the entirety of imperial religious policy.
candidates.biasAndUncertainty: Pro-Athanasius/Alexandrian episcopal perspective; presents events through ecclesiastical legitimacy and repression. The date calculations and interpretation of the translated month names should be checked against a specialist calendar edition before asserting exact civil dates.

candidates.event: Athanasius' death, Peter's succession, and subsequent installation of Lucius under Valens

primarySource.title: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History
primarySource.exactLocator: Book IV.20–22; especially IV.20 (death and Peter) and IV.21 (Lucius installed with imperial troops); IV.22 notes Peter's flight and Socrates' criticism of Sabinus
primarySource.coverageActuallyRead: Read IV.20–22. Socrates gives the death year by consular dating, describes Peter as successor, says Euzoius requested permission while Valens was at Antioch, and reports the use of imperial troops and the Egyptian governor's mandate to install Lucius. IV.22 explicitly accuses Sabinus of concealing abuses and invokes Peter's letters; this is a later author's characterization, not an independently read letter here.
primarySource.sourceDateAsStated: IV.20: ‘second consulate of Gratian and Probus’; no month/day in this passage. IV.21 gives the sequence after the death and says Valens was then at Antioch.
primarySource.editorialDateOrConversion: The consular year is conventionally identified as 373 CE. Do not supply an exact day from this passage. Historia Acephala XII.17 independently gives Pachon 8 and the translation prints May 3, 373; this corroborates the annal date but requires same calendar caveat.
primarySource.narratorDateAndAge: Socrates wrote in the fifth century, decades after the events; exact birth year/age is uncertain, and he is not presented here as eyewitness. The consulted text does not identify his sources for IV.20–21.

localGeography: Antioch (Valens' stated residence at the time)
whatItCanSupport: Athanasius died in the consular year 373 and Peter succeeded him, according to Socrates.
Socrates reports a contested episcopal succession involving Lucius, imperial troops, and the governor of Egypt.
The transition affected church leadership and the emperor's role in ecclesial control.
whatItDoesNotProve: The exact day of death from Socrates IV.20.
That Socrates' loaded labels ‘Arian’/‘orthodox’ are neutral descriptions or that every faction's theology is captured by them.
The factual particulars of abuses Socrates says Peter reported, since the cited letters were not separately consulted here.
That the succession was peaceful or accepted by all Alexandrians.
candidates.biasAndUncertainty: Nicene ecclesiastical narrative strongly favorable to Athanasius/Peter and hostile to Valens' religious policy and Lucius; IV.22 openly accuses a rival historian of concealment. Treat allegations and polemical descriptions as attributed claims.

candidates.event: Battle near Hadrianopolis and death of Valens, with uncertainty explicitly preserved by Ammianus

primarySource.title: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae
primarySource.exactLocator: Book XXXI.12.1–13.19; battle date at XXXI.12.10; outcome at XXXI.13.1 and alternative death accounts at XXXI.13.12–17
primarySource.coverageActuallyRead: Read XXXI.12.1–13.19 in the Rolfe translation hosted by LacusCurtius, including the campaign approach, date phrase, battle, defeat, and conflicting accounts of Valens' death. The same page's Thayer note 124 identifies the date as Aug. 9; note 138 compares Libanius' divergent account and reports that other authorities agree with Ammianus' following account.
primarySource.sourceDateAsStated: XXXI.12.10 says the fifth day before the Ides of August (in the Roman calendar), conventionally August 9; it locates the baggage at Hadrianopolis and the battle at the Goths' wagon encampment after a march over rough ground. The narrative says Valens was killed, body unrecovered (13.1).
primarySource.editorialDateOrConversion: August 9 is the standard conversion of the Roman date. Page note 124 supplies that conversion; distinguish it from the ancient wording. The online translator/editor notes that Ammianus gives mutually inconsistent explanations of Valens' death and says the exact date has a calendar/astronomical tension (note a); preserve source uncertainty rather than resolving it.
primarySource.narratorDateAndAge: Ammianus was a late fourth-century author and former Roman military officer; his exact birth year/age is unknown. His firsthand service in earlier campaigns does not establish eyewitness presence at Adrianople. The passage itself says the report of Valens' fatal arrow wound came from what people supposed and that nobody claimed to have seen him; it then gives a second-hand survivor's account of a cottage fire.

localGeography: Hadrianopolis / Adrianople (modern Edirne, Turkey, geographic identification is modern control)
Thracian plain and route from the imperial villa Melanthias; battle described near the Goths' wagon encampment
whatItCanSupport: Ammianus' narrative of Valens' campaign, battle, Roman defeat, and catastrophic losses.
Ammianus reports the battle date as the fifth before the Ides of August.
Ammianus explicitly preserves competing/unverified accounts of how Valens died and says his body was not found.
whatItDoesNotProve: An exact modern map coordinate for the battlefield or the wagon circle.
A definitive account of Valens' death; Ammianus gives alternatives and admits no witness to one account.
The exact casualty totals beyond Ammianus' own estimates/rhetoric.
A religious-confessional cause for the battle; the passage is military/political narrative, not evidence that the conflict was a doctrinal campaign.
candidates.biasAndUncertainty: Ammianus writes from a Roman elite military perspective and uses strongly literary, moralizing descriptions of opponents and Roman command failures. The account is unusually detailed, but not explicitly eyewitness for this battle; note the author's own alternatives and uncertainties.

candidates.event: Gratian appoints Theodosius co-emperor and Socrates records recalled bishops and church policy

primarySource.title: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History
primarySource.exactLocator: Book V.1–3, especially V.2; accession at V.2, church leadership snapshot at V.3
primarySource.coverageActuallyRead: Read V.1–3. V.2 says Gratian recalled exiled bishops, describes permissions/exclusions for assemblies, and says Theodosius was proclaimed emperor at Sirmium on January 16 in the consulate of Ausonius and Olybrius. V.3 lists church leadership and competing groups in Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople.
primarySource.sourceDateAsStated: V.2 explicitly gives Sirmium and 16 January in the consulate of Ausonius and Olybrius; the consular year is 379. It presents appointment after Valens' death and Gratian's actions.
primarySource.editorialDateOrConversion: The modern year 379 follows the consular dating; the day is stated in the source's translated text. Do not infer a precise chronology for each recall or policy action from this compressed narrative alone.
primarySource.narratorDateAndAge: Socrates is a fifth-century church historian writing retrospectively; exact age at composition is uncertain. No eyewitness claim is made for the appointment.

localGeography: Sirmium (appointment place as stated by Socrates; modern Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia is an identification, not wording in source)
Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Antioch-in-Syria appear as church-status locations in V.3 and V.4
whatItCanSupport: Socrates dates Theodosius' elevation at Sirmium to January 16 in the consulate of Ausonius and Olybrius.
Socrates connects post-Valens political succession with changes concerning recalled bishops and public religious assembly.
Socrates describes continued factional and episcopal complexity rather than a settled uniform landscape.
whatItDoesNotProve: That Theodosius' elevation itself was a religious conversion or immediate empire-wide settlement.
That every detail of Gratian's policy was implemented uniformly across cities.
A complete account of the negotiations, army process, or date of each bishop's return.
That the historian's ‘orthodox/heretic’ classifications are impartial.
candidates.biasAndUncertainty: Nicene ecclesiastical framing; Socrates praises imperial protection of the Nicene party while recording local disagreements. Treat his theological taxonomy and descriptions of policy as his interpretation.

candidates.event: Theodosius' arrival in Constantinople, succession of church authorities, and CTh 16.1.2 addressed to Constantinople's population

primarySource.title: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History; Codex Theodosianus, Book XVI
primarySource.exactLocator: Socrates HE V.6–7 for arrival and church transfer (translation consulted; verify exact chapter heading/paragraph in a critical edition); CTh 16.1.2 for the imperial constitution
primarySource.coverageActuallyRead: Socrates V.2–3 read for accession and church configuration, plus search/open excerpt V.6 lines reporting arrival in Constantinople on November 24 and V.7 lines reporting churches transferred on November 26. The Codex Latin text CTh 16.1.2 was read on Wikisource, including its body and subscription. The Codex is a later compilation (promulgated 438) preserving the earlier constitution; online transcription is not a manuscript inspection.
primarySource.sourceDateAsStated: Socrates V.6 says Theodosius arrived at Constantinople on November 24 in the fifth consulate of Gratian and first of Theodosius; V.7 says church transfer occurred November 26 in that consular year. CTh 16.1.2's subscription says issued at Thessalonica, III Kalends of March, under Gratian's fifth and Theodosius' first consulships (conventionally February 27, 380). It addresses ‘all peoples governed by our clemency’ and invokes communion with named bishops, including Nectarius of Constantinople and Timothy of Egypt.
primarySource.editorialDateOrConversion: 380 and November 24/26 are modern conversions of consular dates in the Socrates translation. CTh's III Kalends of March conventionally converts to February 27, 380. Crucial geography: law issued at Thessalonica, while its addressee is the people under imperial rule; it names Constantinople's bishop and cannot be described as an enactment issued in Constantinople.
primarySource.narratorDateAndAge: Socrates wrote in the fifth century and is retrospective; exact age unknown. The imperial constitution is contemporaneous as an enacted legal text, but survives through the Theodosian Code's 5th-century compilation and later manuscript transmission.

localGeography: Thessalonica (place of issuance in CTh subscription)
Constantinople (Socrates' destination; Nectarius named by constitution; church-transfer episode)
Alexandria/Egypt and other named sees appear in CTh's communion list
whatItCanSupport: Socrates reports Theodosius' arrival in Constantinople and subsequent church possession changes on separately dated days.
CTh 16.1.2 articulates an imperial confessional norm and names episcopal communion partners; its subscription fixes issuance at Thessalonica.
The legal text concerns the status/name of churches and asserted religious affiliation; it is direct evidence of imperial legal language, not a neutral description of social practice.
whatItDoesNotProve: That Christianity became literally the empire's only practiced religion or that the constitution was enforced uniformly everywhere.
That the law was promulgated in Constantinople; the subscription says Thessalonica.
That the church transfer on November 26 followed automatically from CTh 16.1.2; Socrates supplies a separate narrative and dates it later.
That the surviving Codex page is the original issued document or an extant 4th-century manuscript.
A complete account of the First Council of Constantinople (381), which lies outside the selected chronology.
candidates.biasAndUncertainty: Socrates frames events as restoration of Nicene/‘homoousian’ churches and uses confessional categories. The law is an imperial self-presentation with coercive normative language. Do not collapse proclamation, practical enforcement, and later council settlement into one event.

overallLimits: These five candidates are not recommendations to add five episodes or one episode per year; selection and scope remain with the architect.
The historical interval can be covered by fewer or differently framed events; no exhaustive chronological claim is made.
Geographical names are textual place references, not verified archaeological placement or game-map coordinates.
The primary-source excerpts were consulted in online translations/transcriptions; no critical apparatus, manuscript images, or full modern scholarly editions were inspected.
